main.title: Pandora's Tower
main.subtitle: A rescue measured in time away
main.summary: Pandora's Tower is Ganbarion's Wii action role-playing game following Aeron's attempt to save Elena from a curse that is turning her into a monster. He explores thirteen towers in search of the flesh needed to reverse its effects, returning to an observatory where Elena waits. The journey connects combat and environmental puzzles with the condition of someone left behind. Every expedition therefore has a practical urgency: progress deeper into a tower must be weighed against the time that Elena can safely endure before Aeron comes back.

cards.heading: A rescue measured in time away
cards.text: Pandora's Tower is Ganbarion's Wii action role-playing game following Aeron's attempt to save Elena from a curse that is turning her into a monster. He explores thirteen towers in search of the flesh needed to reverse its effects, returning to an observatory where Elena waits. The journey connects combat and environmental puzzles with the condition of someone left behind. Every expedition therefore has a practical urgency: progress deeper into a tower must be weighed against the time that Elena can safely endure before Aeron comes back.

cards.heading: The chain reaches beyond a weapon
cards.text: Aeron's Oraclos Chain binds enemies, pulls away armour and connects targets so that damage can be shared between them. Its usefulness extends into the towers' architecture, allowing him to grapple, climb and swing across gaps. A mechanism or platform can become another part of the same tool's vocabulary. The tower Masters remain locked behind environmental challenges, so reaching a boss involves understanding the route as well as surviving it. Combat and exploration continually ask the player to reconsider what can be caught, pulled or connected by the chain.

cards.heading: A return changes the relationship
cards.text: Bringing flesh to Elena reverses the curse for a time, but its usefulness deteriorates after it is collected. Talking with her, giving gifts and asking for help with tasks also affect the relationship recorded by the game. The observatory is therefore more than an equipment stop between battles. It is the place where the expedition's purpose becomes visible and where time spent together has consequences. Different endings respond to that bond, connecting the larger outcome with the pattern of departures, discoveries and returns made throughout the adventure.

main.title: inFAMOUS 2
main.subtitle: Find enough power to face the Beast
main.summary: inFAMOUS 2 is Sucker Punch Productions' PlayStation 3 action-adventure, released in North America on 7 June 2011. Cole MacGrath reaches New Marais after confronting a threat known as the Beast. He must develop his electrical powers before their next encounter, navigating a city inspired by New Orleans. Its streets, rooftops and waterways provide both routes and battlegrounds. The sequel continues Cole's story while giving his movement more room, making the journey across an urban district part of the pleasure of reaching the next mission.

cards.heading: Find enough power to face the Beast
cards.text: inFAMOUS 2 is Sucker Punch Productions' PlayStation 3 action-adventure, released in North America on 7 June 2011. Cole MacGrath reaches New Marais after confronting a threat known as the Beast. He must develop his electrical powers before their next encounter, navigating a city inspired by New Orleans. Its streets, rooftops and waterways provide both routes and battlegrounds. The sequel continues Cole's story while giving his movement more room, making the journey across an urban district part of the pleasure of reaching the next mission.

cards.heading: Use the city as a circuit
cards.text: Cole climbs buildings, crosses gaps and uses electrical infrastructure to move through the city. His powers support ranged attacks and close fighting, while the Amp adds a dedicated melee weapon. Electricity also supplies a resource to replenish, connecting combat to the objects and routes around him. Rather than remaining a backdrop, the city provides places to draw power and ways to approach an encounter from another height. Growing abilities change the ease of those movements, letting an increasingly powerful Cole cross spaces that once required a more cautious route.

cards.heading: A choice changes the kind of hero
cards.text: Karma decisions again divide Cole's development between helpful and selfish uses of power. They affect available abilities, the response of people in the city and the direction of the story. The sequel also included tools for making and sharing user-created missions, extending the activities available within New Marais. Director Nate Fox returned, while the music drew on the sound of the city that inspired the setting. Its combination of traversal, combat and moral choices brought Cole's journey to two sharply different possible conclusions in the main campaign.

main.title: Bastion
main.summary: Bastion is a 2011 action role-playing video game developed by independent developer Supergiant Games and originally published by Warner Bros.

cards.heading: The Kid after the Calamity
cards.text: Bastion is a 2011 action role-playing video game developed by independent developer Supergiant Games and originally published by Warner Bros. Interactive Entertainment. In the game, the player controls "the Kid" as he moves through floating, fantasy-themed environments and fights enemies of various types. It features a dynamic voiceover from a narrator (Logan Cunningham), and is presented as a two-dimensional game with an isometric camera and a hand-painted art style. Bastion's story follows the Kid as he collects special shards of rock to power a structure, the Bastion, in the wake of an apocalyptic Calamity.

cards.heading: Seven developers and a growing audience
cards.text: The game was built over the course of two years by a team of seven people split between San Jose and New York City. They introduced the game at the September 2010 Penny Arcade Expo, and it went on to be nominated for awards at the 2011 Independent Games Festival and win awards at the Electronic Entertainment Expo prior to release. Bastion was published in July 2011 for Xbox 360 via Xbox Live Arcade, and in August 2011 through digital distribution for Microsoft Windows on Steam. Supergiant Games made it available as a browser game for Google Chrome in December 2011. It was released for Mac OS X and iOS in 2012, for PlayStation 4 and PlayStation Vita in 2015, for Xbox One in 2016, and Nintendo Switch in 2018. Bastion's soundtrack was produced and composed by Darren Korb, and a soundtrack album was made available for sale in August 2011.

cards.heading: The response to Bastion
cards.text: During 2011, the game sold more than 500,000 copies, 200,000 of which were for the Xbox Live Arcade. It sold over three million copies across all platforms by January 2015. The game was widely praised by reviewers, primarily for its story, art direction, narration, and music. Opinions were mixed on the depth of the gameplay, though the variety of options in the combat system was praised. Bastion has won many nominations and awards since its release, including several for best downloadable game and best music, from review outlets such as IGN and Game Informer as well as from the Spike Video Game Awards, the Game Developers Conference, and the Academy of Interactive Arts & Sciences.

features.title: Darren Korb and Ashley Barrett
features.summary: Darren Korb's compositions, Ashley Barrett's singing and Logan Cunningham's narration give Bastion several distinct voices.

cards.heading: The composer and the singers
cards.text: Darren Korb wrote, produced and recorded Bastion's original soundtrack, released on 5 August 2011. Its credits also identify the singers of individual songs. Ashley Barrett performs Build That Wall, while Korb sings Mother, I'm Here. Composition, production and performance are different parts of the same recording: Korb's role as the album's composer does not mean that every voice on it is his. Barrett's performance gives one of the soundtrack's central songs its own identifiable voice.

cards.heading: Two voices meet in the ending
cards.text: Barrett and Korb sing together on Setting Sail, Coming Home, the ending theme. The album therefore includes both their individual performances and a shared song. Its credits also name Greg Kasavin as the lyricist of Get Used to It and Logan Cunningham as its vocalist. Following those credits reveals a collaboration rather than a soundtrack made by one person alone. Listening to the solo songs and then the ending offers a way to hear the different voices within the same musical world.

cards.heading: Logan Cunningham's narrator
cards.text: Logan Cunningham is also the voice of Bastion's narrator, Rucks. Supergiant describes narration that reacts to the player's actions as the Kid travels through the world and rebuilds the refuge. The spoken narration and the songs belong to the same game, but work differently: the narrator responds to events during play, while the soundtrack album presents fixed recordings. Cunningham's spoken presence therefore forms another part of Bastion's vocal identity alongside Barrett's and Korb's singing.

cards.heading: From recordings to playable arrangements
cards.text: On 15 March 2012, Greg Kasavin announced official guitar and piano arrangements of four Bastion songs. Supergiant explained that listeners had requested tabs and sheet music since the game's debut, and offered the collection free of charge as thanks for their support. These arrangements provided a different way to engage with the soundtrack: playing the songs rather than only hearing the recordings. The publication followed the original 2011 release and connected the game's music with an audience who wanted to perform it.

main.title: The Stanley Parable
main.summary: Davey Wreden’s original Half-Life 2 modification explores what happens when a player follows, questions or disobeys an unseen narrator.

cards.heading: A narrator to disobey
cards.text: Davey Wreden created The Stanley Parable as a Half-Life 2 mod. Its unseen narrator describes a path for the player, who can follow the account or act against it. Wreden began considering the idea about three years before release, prompted by questions he felt many games left unanswered when players tried something outside the intended story.

cards.heading: A design built on questions
cards.text: Though his initial intent was a personal project simply to try to make such a game that asked the questions about why people play video games, Wreden found that there were other gamers that had been considering the same type of questions. He set out to make a game that would be the subject of discussion for players after they completed it. According to Wreden, his design document for the game was "Mess with the player's head in every way possible, throwing them off-guard, or pretending there's an answer and then kinda whisking it away from in front of them." Wreden decided to use an "unconventional narrator" in order to work with the idea of what would happen if the player elected to disobey the narrator.

cards.heading: Teaching himself Source
cards.text: Wreden taught himself Source using SDK wikis and forums. He developed the mod alone apart from Kevan Brighting's narration, selected through auditions. Keeping it short let players try several endings without repeating a lengthy adventure, and gave the writing room for abrupt or absurd conclusions.

cards.heading: When a broken puzzle became meaningful
cards.text: Most of the ideas he had envisioned for the game were included, though some had to be dropped due to his inability to figure out how to work with them within the Source engine. In one case, Wreden wanted to include a point where the player would have to press buttons as the narration and screen prompts would have said, but could not figure out how to bind keyboard input to do this, but left the element in there as a "broken" puzzle; he later was praised for this, as to players, this gave the impression of lacking control during the stage of narration. Despite the success of completing the game, Wreden considered the overall project "grueling" and stifling of his career ambition, noting that his efforts became more intense once he started learning of other players' interest in the title.

cards.heading: From a mod to a new project
cards.text: Wreden initially tested the game with a friend before posting the mod to the website ModDB on July 31, 2011, a few weeks prior to his graduation from college. After graduating, Wreden had left for Australia with intent to open a video game-themed bar similar to the Mana Bar, which he had worked at for about a year, but his future plans changed with success of the mod. Wreden had started to receive various offers from others to help work on new games as well as some job offers from larger developers which he turned down, as at the time it was "not the kind of scene" he wanted to work in. Instead, he started to gather other independent programmers to work out an improved version of The Stanley Parable and leading towards a completely new title in the future.

main.title: Kirby Mass Attack
main.summary: The stylus directs up to ten small Kirbies, with fruit building the group and rescue gestures keeping its members from floating away.

cards.heading: The game
cards.text: Kirby Mass Attack is HAL Laboratory's 2011 Nintendo DS action-platform game. Necrodeus splits Kirby into ten small versions of himself, and the player guides the growing group with the stylus. Its puzzles and fights depend on gathering enough Kirbies, moving them together and keeping the group healthy as the journey continues.

cards.heading: Point the group towards the problem
cards.text: Touching the screen places a star that the Kirbies follow; a double tap sends them running towards a point. Flicking a Kirby launches him into a jump, which can also break a block or start an attack. Once several pile onto an enemy, they begin fighting automatically, and more taps help the group overpower it. The controls turn a small patch of screen into several possible orders: gather here, rush there, or send one member towards an object above the others.

cards.heading: Every Kirby changes the possibilities
cards.text: Fruit fills a gauge that adds another Kirby to the group, up to a maximum of ten. Larger numbers make fights and tug-of-war obstacles easier and allow entry into stages that require a particular group size. Damage turns a Kirby blue; another hit sends him floating away as an angel. Flicking a healthy companion upwards to catch him brings him back before he is lost. Protecting the group therefore involves small rescue decisions as well as choosing where everyone should go next.

cards.heading: Look beyond the exit
cards.text: Medals hidden through the stages encourage searching beyond the most direct route. Collecting them opens extra games, while Daroach's airship offers hints about treasures that remain to be found. The extras give Kirby another set of roles, including pinball and shooting challenges, alongside the main adventure's group puzzles. A stage cleared with a healthy crowd may still have a medal tucked behind an obstacle, giving the next visit a specific purpose and rewarding closer attention to the room's layout.

main.title: Deus Ex: Human Revolution
main.summary: Deus Ex: Human Revolution is an action role-playing game developed by Eidos-Montréal and published by Square Enix.

cards.heading: Adam Jensen and human augmentation
cards.text: Deus Ex: Human Revolution is an action role-playing game developed by Eidos-Montréal and published by Square Enix. The game is a prequel to the original Deus Ex (2000) and the third installment in the Deus Ex series. The gameplay combines first-person shooter, stealth, and role-playing elements. It features exploration and combat in environments connected to multiple city-based hubs, in addition to quests that grant experience and allow customization of the main character's abilities with items called Praxis Kits. Set in the year 2027, players control Adam Jensen, a security officer for Sarif Industries, a company which develops controversial artificial organs dubbed "augmentations". After an attack on Sarif, Jensen undergoes extensive augmentation and investigates the shadowy organization behind the attack. The story explores themes of transhumanism and the growing power of megacorporations and their impact on social class. It also uses the series' cyberpunk setting and conspiracy theory motif.

cards.heading: Icarus, the Renaissance and cyberpunk
cards.text: Development of Human Revolution began in 2007 with a small team within the fledgling Eidos-Montréal studio after failed attempts to create a sequel at original developer Ion Storm following Deus Ex: Invisible War (2003). The two key influences were the myth of Icarus, a thematic element carried over from Deus Ex, and the artwork and ideas of the Renaissance, which influenced the story, graphics, and music while combining with the series' typical cyberpunk elements. The open-ended gameplay was tricky for the team to achieve; the boss battles were outsourced to another developer due to time constraints. The music, composed by Michael McCann, focused on ambience and three-layered compositions over character themes and overt melodies. Human Revolution was announced in 2007, soon after its beginning development. Its title and release window were announced in 2010.

cards.heading: The original release and its legacy
cards.text: Human Revolution was released for PlayStation 3, Windows, and Xbox 360 in August 2011. The game received critical acclaim for its player-driven plot, gameplay, and freedom of choice in the story and character customization. The major criticisms went to its boss fights and technical problems. The director's cut was praised for its revamped gameplay. By November 2011, the original version had sold 2.18 million units. After release, a downloadable episode, The Missing Link, was developed, featuring gameplay improvements. A director's cut, featuring further improvements and additional content, was released in October 2013 for the original platforms and Wii U. The game was followed up with a spin-off, The Fall in 2013, and a direct sequel, Mankind Divided in 2016.

main.title: Resistance 3
main.subtitle: Crossing a country after the defeat
main.summary: Resistance 3 is Insomniac Games' PlayStation 3 first-person shooter, released in North America on 6 September 2011. Joseph Capelli leaves his family and a hidden community to travel toward New York with scientist Fyodor Malikov. The Chimera have already devastated human civilisation, shifting the story from an organised military response toward survival and a dangerous journey. Towns and hostile landscapes become individual stops rather than parts of another victorious campaign. Capelli's reason to continue is personal, giving the war a smaller human centre even when its consequences remain enormous.

cards.heading: Crossing a country after the defeat
cards.text: Resistance 3 is Insomniac Games' PlayStation 3 first-person shooter, released in North America on 6 September 2011. Joseph Capelli leaves his family and a hidden community to travel toward New York with scientist Fyodor Malikov. The Chimera have already devastated human civilisation, shifting the story from an organised military response toward survival and a dangerous journey. Towns and hostile landscapes become individual stops rather than parts of another victorious campaign. Capelli's reason to continue is personal, giving the war a smaller human centre even when its consequences remain enormous.

cards.heading: Carry the arsenal and keep it useful
cards.text: The weapon wheel returns, letting Capelli carry a broad selection rather than choosing only two guns. Familiar Chimeran designs sit alongside new equipment, and weapons improve through use. The player can therefore respond to an encounter by changing the tool instead of waiting to find another one. A health bar and recovery items also return, making supplies and the aftermath of a fight matter between attacks. Explosive environmental objects provide further options, turning the position of enemies and nearby hazards into part of selecting a shot.

cards.heading: A journey that another player can share
cards.text: The campaign supports cooperative play, including local split-screen, so a second player can accompany the trip through the ruined country. PlayStation Move and stereoscopic 3D were also supported, extending the ways the same adventure could be presented and controlled. Marcus Smith directed, Drew Murray led design and Boris Salchow composed the score. Reviewers generally welcomed the more focused journey and returning arsenal. The game became Insomniac's final Resistance entry, and Sony closed its online servers with those of the earlier PlayStation 3 games in April 2014.

main.title: Tales of Xillia
main.subtitle: Two convictions lead into the same conflict
main.summary: Tales of Xillia is Namco Tales Studio's PlayStation 3 action role-playing game, first released in Japan in September 2011. Jude Mathis and Milla Maxwell become fugitives after interfering with the Lance of Kresnik, a weapon threatening the relationship between humans and spirits. The player chooses a lead viewpoint, following a party whose members arrive with different commitments and experiences. Exploration moves into active battles, while conversations between the group give the journey a more personal rhythm. The story's larger conflict is carried through the relationship between two protagonists who understand their responsibility in different ways.

cards.heading: Two convictions lead into the same conflict
cards.text: Tales of Xillia is Namco Tales Studio's PlayStation 3 action role-playing game, first released in Japan in September 2011. Jude Mathis and Milla Maxwell become fugitives after interfering with the Lance of Kresnik, a weapon threatening the relationship between humans and spirits. The player chooses a lead viewpoint, following a party whose members arrive with different commitments and experiences. Exploration moves into active battles, while conversations between the group give the journey a more personal rhythm. The story's larger conflict is carried through the relationship between two protagonists who understand their responsibility in different ways.

cards.heading: Link two fighters so the party acts together
cards.text: The battle system lets party members form links that provide support and lead into coordinated actions. A character's immediate attacks therefore belong to a relationship with somebody else on the field. The player changes the pairing to suit the encounter, considering both the controlled fighter and the assistance available around them. Outside battle, voiced skits give companions room to react to events and one another. These smaller exchanges help make the group more than a collection of combat roles, connecting the practical cooperation of a fight to the personalities travelling together between encounters.

cards.heading: A meeting of two Tales artists
cards.text: Kōsuke Fujishima and Mutsumi Inomata both contributed character designs, bringing together artists closely associated with different parts of Tales. Motoi Sakuraba composed the music, while Naoto Miyadera directed and Hideo Baba produced. Western editions arrived in August 2013 after a strong Japanese reception and substantial sales. A direct sequel followed in Japan in 2012, and a later remaster returned the original adventure to more platforms. Xillia's defining contribution is the pairing at its centre, expressed through both the story's viewpoints and a combat system that makes one fighter's actions more useful through another.

main.title: The Gunstringer
main.subtitle: Pull the strings of an undead cowboy
main.summary: The Gunstringer is Twisted Pixel's Xbox 360 Kinect shooting game, first released in North America on 13 September 2011. An undead marionette sheriff rises to take revenge on the gang that betrayed him, with the story presented as a theatrical performance. The player uses hand movements rather than a gamepad: one hand guides the puppet while the other aims its gun. Live-action footage of an audience frames the adventure as a show, making the person in front of the television both performer and puppeteer within the same comic Western.

cards.heading: Pull the strings of an undead cowboy
cards.text: The Gunstringer is Twisted Pixel's Xbox 360 Kinect shooting game, first released in North America on 13 September 2011. An undead marionette sheriff rises to take revenge on the gang that betrayed him, with the story presented as a theatrical performance. The player uses hand movements rather than a gamepad: one hand guides the puppet while the other aims its gun. Live-action footage of an audience frames the adventure as a show, making the person in front of the television both performer and puppeteer within the same comic Western.

cards.heading: Point, mark and make the firing gesture
cards.text: The aiming hand can select several enemies before a firing gesture sends the Gunstringer's shots towards them. Movement of the other hand guides the character through the action, translating the image of a suspended puppet into the control scheme. Some sections follow a fixed route and allow both hands to operate guns. The player therefore alternates between directing the figure and concentrating on the targets ahead. Kinect's body tracking becomes useful because the fiction explains the gesture: the hand is not pretending to hold a conventional controller but manipulating a character on a stage.

cards.heading: A small digital idea becomes a retail performance
cards.text: The project began as an Xbox Live Arcade game before being expanded into a full retail release. Its four acts follow different members of the former gang through exaggerated Western settings, mixing stage scenery with modern and supernatural jokes. Edward Kuehnel wrote the story for a game whose presentation makes room for both the puppet and the audience watching it. The Gunstringer became one of Kinect's more distinctive experiments by giving the input a clear theatrical purpose. The player's moving hands belong naturally to a story about a marionette finding its way across the stage.

main.title: Tekken Tag Tournament 2
main.summary: Tekken Tag Tournament 2 is a 2011 fighting game, the eighth installment in the Tekken fighting game series and the sequel to Tekken Tag Tournament.

cards.heading: From arcades to home consoles
cards.text: Tekken Tag Tournament 2 is a 2011 fighting game, the eighth installment in the Tekken fighting game series and the sequel to Tekken Tag Tournament. It was released for the arcades in September 2011. It received an update, subtitled Unlimited, in March 2012. A console version based on the update was released for PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360 in September 2012. It was ported to the Wii U as one of the system's launch titles in November 2012, subtitled Wii U Edition.

cards.heading: A large roster and a mixed outcome
cards.text: As with the original Tekken Tag Tournament (1999), the game includes almost every character from past Tekken games, giving it the largest playable roster in a Tekken game to date. Players can choose either a team of two characters on each side or a solo character. Tekken Tag Tournament 2 has been positively received by critics, earning averaged review scores in the range of 82-83% at both GameRankings and Metacritic for the PlayStation 3, Wii U and Xbox 360 versions, as well as several fighting-game-of-the-year awards. However, the game sold at a historic low for the main series, affecting budgets in the succeeding games, especially Tekken 7.
